anatomy.title: Three things. No more.
anatomy.lead: Every AI project that actually sticks breaks down into the same three parts. Understand those and you can judge for yourself what a tool does and does not do for you.
anatomy.card1Body: Your documentation, tone of voice, examples and policy. Not vague training data — concrete files you manage yourself.
anatomy.card2Body: One document with rules, exceptions and goals. Readable by colleagues, executable by the model. Not a 47-step flowchart.
anatomy.card3Body: Concrete actions: draft an email, look up an invoice, prepare a meeting. Nothing beyond what you allow. With an audit log and human review.

model.title1: An agent is not a product.
model.lead: Once you understand what an agent is made of, you can build, debug and extend one yourself. We teach you the pattern.
model.card1Body: One folder with markdown files. Documentation, policies, examples, tone of voice. Versionable in git, editable by anyone.
model.card2Body: One readable document. Goals, rules, edge cases and escalation paths. No YAML spaghetti, no 47-step flowchart.
model.card3Body: Functions in your own code. Send mail, create a ticket, look up an invoice. With permissions, audit log and human review where it counts.

process.title: Four phases. Your team is on board the whole way.
process.lead: We don't build for you — we build with you. Otherwise you end up with a tool nobody understands six months from now.
process.step1Body: We map 1-3 use cases. Which fits an agent, which is just a script? What's the value, what are the risks?
process.step2Body: The team building or maintaining the agent gets the foundation first. Folder, instructions, tools — no magic.
process.step3Body: Pair-building. We steer, you type. Or vice versa. First working version in weeks, not quarters.
process.step4Body: Handover, runbook, monitoring. What do you do if it gets something wrong? Who approves new versions?

trifecta.lead: A term from Simon Willison. An agent that has all three of these properties at once is a prompt-injection target. We design our agents so at least one is always missing — or so there's a human in the loop at the point where it matters.
trifecta.card1Body: The agent reads your documents, customer list, CRM, email threads. Fine on its own — until you add 2 and 3.
trifecta.card2Body: Web pages, customer uploads, third-party emails, scraped data. An attacker can hide instructions in there which the agent will follow.
trifecta.card3Body: The agent can reach out: send mail, call APIs, post messages. The channel an attacker uses to exfiltrate your data.
trifecta.footer: Combine all three and you've built a data-exfiltration pipeline. We design every agent explicitly to prevent that — separated capabilities, an audit log per tool call, human approval on the dangerous steps.

items.q: Do you also offer open trainings?
items.a: No. We only work in-company. Training really lands when participants can work on their own use cases with colleagues.

items.q: What's the minimum number of participants?

list.title: A ServiceNow agent that works from the terminal
list.summary: Serac is a terminal agent for ServiceNow developers and consultants: build, analyse and deploy from the command line, with 429 ServiceNow tools exposed over MCP. You bring your own AI provider and your own instance, so there is no third party in the chain.
list.why: A monorepo of roughly eighteen packages, with build and plan agents whose permissions you set per step. Apache 2.0, installable via npm, Homebrew, Scoop, Choco and AUR — you can check what it does before pointing it at your instance.

list.title: From free tool to a paid platform in production
list.summary: A commercial platform runs around the free agent: hosted runtime, licence keys and connectors to Jira, Azure DevOps, Confluence, GitHub and GitLab. Credentials sit encrypted in a dedicated vault, with white-label portals and an on-prem variant for those who want nothing leaving the building.

outcomes.label: tools on top of the free CLI

list.why: Open source proves it works; a platform around it makes it usable for organisations that do not want to run a CLI. AES-256-GCM for customer credentials, because that is exactly the kind of data you do not treat casually.

list.title: Case management for the Dutch Tweede Spoor track
list.summary: DIM runs the entire Tweede Spoor reintegration track through one platform. The statutory steps and the UWV weekly cadence live in the data model itself, not in agreements alongside the system.
list.why: Isolation between case files via Postgres Row-Level Security rather than carefully written queries — the latter goes wrong eventually. And after phase 1 is paid, code, data and infrastructure transfer fully to DIM. No lock-in, even where lock-in would have been commercially convenient.

list.title: Meeting audio straight to draft minutes
list.summary: Turning a recording into minutes is work nobody enjoys. Snelnotuleren.nl did it automatically: audio in, transcript and draft minutes out, plus a chat over the transcript to find details again.
list.why: Four microservices with CI/CD to Cloud Run and separate test and prod branches. I wound it down deliberately rather than letting it linger — a product you no longer maintain is one you should stop selling.

list.title: Repair reports gathered by phone and WhatsApp
list.summary: At a property management firm every repair report had to be called back and worked through by hand. The agent calls the reporter itself or handles it over WhatsApp, works through the report in a structured way and writes the data straight through. Running in production.
list.why: Both channels share the same tool definitions and prompts, so a change to the questions applies to both at once. The telephony side has hand-written mu-law/PCM16 conversion and answering machine detection — that kind of detail decides whether it works in practice. The client stays unnamed; the work does not.

list.title: Tailoring CVs to the vacancy, with open code
list.summary: Retailoring a CV for every vacancy takes time. CVeetje does it with AI: bring your own encrypted AI key or pay per credit, and get your CV back in your own template.
list.why: The code is deliberately open source so users can verify their data stays in their own Firebase project. Flat PDFs without form fields go through a vision route that fills the document as an overlay — the awkward cases are the whole point.

list.title: An AI checkout that pays with a signed mandate
list.role: First integration with a real PSP
list.summary: Google's Agent Payments Protocol describes how an AI agent may pay on someone's behalf. This integration connects it to Mollie. You approve once; the agent handles the payment after that, with a cryptographically signed mandate chain as proof of exactly what was allowed.
list.why: Four agents — orchestrator, shopping, mandate, payment — and the full chain from intent to payment signed as JWT. An agent that spends money without an audit trail is not a product, it is a liability.

list.title: Scaffolding new agents to one fixed pattern
list.summary: Every agent used to start as its own construction: different folder layout, different way of handling credentials, different conventions. The meta-agent asks six questions and then lays down a complete agent folder to one recorded architecture.

outcomes.label: self-driving loops came out of it

list.why: File-based and model-agnostic, no web app or dashboard. There is a dry run before anything is written, and cost logging for runs that happen without a human. This is exactly what I teach teams: structure first, tooling after.

list.title: An agent that picks up issues, behind a test gate
list.summary: Small bugs kept sliding because they were too small to plan. This loop runs every working day, picks up labelled issues, opens a branch and a draft PR, and sends a separate reviewer pass over it. A per-repo gate decides what may happen next.
list.why: Sensitive areas — auth, payments, credentials, migrations, multi-tenant — are never merged automatically. And the reviewer may never merge its own PR. Autonomy is only useful once you have drawn the line where it stops.

list.title: A site that handles its own quotes, payments and invoices
list.summary: The site you are on is not a brochure, it is the product. Visitors ask a chatbot that searches the site's own content, request a quote that is drafted automatically, and pay through Mollie after which invoicing follows on its own.
list.why: Every branch gets a tagged Cloud Run preview revision that is tested end to end before anything goes live. That is the same discipline I set up at clients — it would be odd not to run it on my own site.

niels.para1Pre: I've been building since models were called 'GPT-3'. First for myself, then for clients. What I learned in those years: technology is almost never the problem. It's about
niels.para2: That's why GroeimetAI is deliberately small. No funnel, no pipeline. Just personal work with teams that genuinely want to change something — and understand it takes time.
niels.para3: Alongside client work I make open source. Serac is the most visible example: an agent framework for ServiceNow that I started for one client and then put on GitHub under Elastic v2. If I promise clients no lock-in, I have to live by it.

beliefs.title: Five things we don't change.

We build on the most appropriate stack, not on the one we earn commission from (we don't get any anyway).
If you can't read it after handover, our work isn't done.
If one training turns you into the builders, that always beats handing over a finished product.
We don't grow for the sake of growth. We want to stay sharp, not scalable.
